title: Gobekli Tepe and its ring of stone circles
site_name: Gobekli Tepe and its ring of stone circles
excerpt: Gobekli Tepe near Sanliurfa presents carved limestone pillars and megalithic enclosures from the Pre
content:
Gobekli Tepe near Sanliurfa is a prehistoric hill site of carved limestone enclosures and T-shaped pillars. Its World Heritage listing in 2018 fixed a place already central to the early story of monumental building.

Pre-Pottery Neolithic enclosures on a limestone ridge

The site lies in south-eastern Anatolia, in the Germu? mountains, where a limestone plateau rises into a low ridge. The surviving monuments belong to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic, between 9,600 and 8,200 BCE, and were erected by hunter-gatherers.

That dating gives Gobekli Tepe its historical weight, but the visible fabric matters as much as the chronology. The enclosures are monumental and megalithic, with round-oval and rectangular forms that sit close to the bedrock.

Carved pillars, animal reliefs and a second architectural phase

Many of the pillars are T-shaped and cut from limestone. Some carry images of wild animals, including repeated reliefs that turn the stone into a surface for carving rather than a plain support.

The site includes a later phase as well, with smaller rectangular structures. This sequence gives the hill its layered character, from large ceremonial enclosures to tighter built forms above them.

World Heritage status and the site’s longer significance

Gobekli Tepe was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2018 under criteria (i), (ii) and (iv). The listing places it among the most important archaeological sites for understanding early monumental architecture.

The inscriptions and official descriptions link the site to Upper Mesopotamia and to a broad transition in human history. Gobekli Tepe stands as an early, built landscape of stone, relief and enclosure, not as a settlement of houses.

Visiting Gobekli Tepe: what travellers from Western Europe should know

  • The site lies in the province of Sanliurfa, in south-eastern Turkey. It is associated with the Germu? mountains and the limestone plateau above Upper Mesopotamia.
  • The terrain is an archaeological hillside with stone-built structures and uneven ground. The monuments sit partly below the surrounding surface, so the site reads as layered earth and masonry rather than a single open square.
  • The official language is Turkish and the currency is the Turkish lira.
  • Entry requirements depend on your nationality; UK travellers can check the FCDO travel advice at gov.uk/foreign-travel-advice, Irish travellers the Department of Foreign Affairs at ireland.ie.

Frequently asked questions about Gobekli Tepe

Where is Gobekli Tepe?

Gobekli Tepe is in Sanliurfa province in south-eastern Turkey, in the Germu? mountains. It belongs to the broader landscape of Upper Mesopotamia.

What appears on site?

The place is an archaeological mound with monumental stone enclosures, carved T-shaped pillars and rectangular remains. The surfaces include reliefs of wild animals and other carved imagery.

What makes Gobekli Tepe distinctive?

Its earliest monuments belong to the Pre-Pottery Neolithic and were made by hunter-gatherers. The site combines early monumental architecture, carved limestone and a 2018 World Heritage inscription.
